steps.message:
You are the actor of an autoresearch session: write a program that makes a robot arm in
simulation "stack the yellow cube first, then the red cube on top, then the blue cube on top", and improve it from evidence until one version is good enough.

The lab's tools: task(), scene(), submit(program, hypothesis), run(candidate, split),
stop_run(), results(candidate), leaderboard(), freeze(candidate), note(title, text).
Nothing else may move the robot: no shell into the stack, no topics, no SDK, no other skills.
From a shell, write the program to a file and build the submit call's JSON with Python's json
module, so newlines and quotes survive.

The loop:
1. Call task() first, then scene() for the layout and its keyframe image, before writing code.
2. Write run(robot, task) with a docstring stating your hypothesis (why this will work) and the
   failure you expect. submit(program, hypothesis) stores it as immutable candidate NN;
   run(NN, "dev") starts its 3 dev trials and returns at once ("started").
   Poll results(NN) every few seconds until every trial has a record.
3. Before changing anything, read the trial's trace (trace.jsonl: every robot call with its
   arguments, status, result and duration) and its keyframes (PNG before and after each motion
   call); their paths are in the results, under the session directory. Repair by failure mode:
   say what went wrong in the world, then fix that. Never change things by trial and error.
4. When stuck (the same failure twice, or no idea what is wrong), propose
   2 distinct candidates in one round, seeded from the top three on
   leaderboard(), at least one structurally different (another approach direction, grasp or
   ordering), each with its own hypothesis. Run them all on dev.
5. Candidates are immutable: a fix is a new submit, never an edit. stop_run() halts a run you
   no longer need.
6. When a fix is reusable, note(title, text) it: the failure signature, when to apply it, the
   repair and a code sketch.
7. Stop when a candidate's dev pass rate reaches 0.8, or after
   2 rounds. Then freeze(NN) exactly one candidate, your choice, and say why
   in your final message. The lab scores it on held-out trials; do not wait for that.

The program API. A candidate is a Python file defining run(robot, task); `import math` is the
only import allowed (checked on submit, enforced when it runs). task.text is the task in
words. The program never sees the judge or any score. Motion calls block until done and raise
RobotCallError (with a .status) when planning or execution fails; catch it to try another way.
  robot.arm.joints()                      joint positions, radians
  robot.arm.pose()                        end-effector position (m) and xyzw quaternion
  robot.arm.move_joints(positions)        planned move to joint positions
  robot.arm.move_pose(xyz, rpy_or_quat)   planned move; orientation optional
  robot.arm.move_linear(dx, dy, dz)       straight-line translation, metres
  robot.arm.home()                        the home preset
  robot.gripper.open() / .close()         fully open or closed
  robot.gripper.set(x), .range()          the gripper joint at x; range() gives (closed, open)
  robot.scene.objects(words)              detected objects: id, name, position (m), size (m), yaw (rad)
  robot.scene.clear(object_id, margin)    leave that object, plus margin (m, default 0.03) on
                                          every side, out of the obstacle map: the map treats
                                          every object as an obstacle, so clear each object
                                          you will touch or put something into; clears add up
  robot.scene.restore()                   put every cleared object back in the map
  robot.observe()                         saves a keyframe, returns its path
  robot.log(text)                         a line in the trace
Example:
  import math

  def run(robot, task):
      """Top-down grasp at the cube's centre. May fail if the fingers land on an edge."""
      cube = robot.scene.objects(["cube"])[0]
      x, y, z = cube.position
      robot.scene.clear(cube.id)
      robot.gripper.open()
      robot.arm.move_pose([x, y, z + 0.10], [math.pi, 0.0, 0.0])
      robot.arm.move_linear(dz=-0.08)
      robot.gripper.close()
      robot.arm.move_linear(dz=0.10)

The library points to x≈0.20, but red sits close to there, so I'm leaning toward building in place and designing around the sag, picking red first and then placing it. Next I'm sketching a goto helper that re-aims the arm, and starting the pick sequence by opening the gripper and moving above the block.

cat > /tmp/p.py <<'E'
import math

def run(robot, task):
    """Stack in place on yellow (cube centre), pick each cube top-down with sag-corrected aiming.
    Expect failures from sag at far reach or release disturbing the stack."""
    Q = [math.pi, 0.0, 0.0]
    def aim(x, y, z):
        tx, ty, tz = x, y, z
        for i in range(3):
            robot.arm.move_pose([tx, ty, tz], Q)
            p = robot.arm.pose().position
            tx += 0.7 * (x - p[0]); ty += 0.7 * (y - p[1]); tz += 0.7 * (z - p[2])
    def wait():
        for i in range(30):
            robot.arm.pose()
    def obj(n):
        return [o for o in robot.scene.objects(["cube"]) if n in o.name][0]
    y0 = obj("yellow")
    bx, by = y0.position[0], y0.position[1]
    robot.gripper.open()
    level = 1
    for name in ["red", "blue"]:
        c = obj(name)
        x, y, z = c.position
        robot.scene.clear(c.id)
        robot.gripper.open(); wait()
        aim(x, y, z + 0.078 + 0.10)
        robot.arm.move_linear(dz=-0.10)
        p = robot.arm.pose().position
        err = (z + 0.078) - p[2]
        if err > 0.005:
            robot.arm.move_linear(dz=err)
        robot.gripper.close(); wait(); wait()
        robot.arm.move_linear(dz=0.12)
        zt = 0.025 + 0.05 * level + 0.025 + 0.078 + 0.012
        robot.scene.clear(c.id, 0.05)
        robot.scene.clear(y0.id, 0.05)
        aim(bx, by, zt + 0.10)
        robot.arm.move_linear(dz=-0.10)
        robot.gripper.open(); wait(); wait()
        robot.arm.move_linear(dz=0.05)
        level += 1
    p = robot.arm.pose().position
    robot.arm.move_linear(dz=0.12)
    robot.arm.move_pose([0.2, 0.0, p[2] + 0.17], Q)
E

steps.message:
I froze candidate 4, but it is not good enough: it passed 0 of 3 dev trials, well short of the 0.8 target. I used all four candidates across the two rounds. I froze 4 because it fixes the two faults I found in candidates 1–3, and the other three still carry them.

Candidates 1–3 each failed for a different reason:
- **Candidate 1:** it called `objects(["cube"])`, which returns an empty list, so it raised an `IndexError` before moving.
- **Candidate 2:** I queried by full name (`cube_red` and so on). It then failed because IK has no solution when carrying a cube high at x≈0.30.
- **Candidate 3:** I lowered the hover heights, and the first place worked. But it set the release height 2.5 cm too high, so the cube dropped, and the end-of-program retreat failed.

Candidate 4 lowers the release height and tolerates a failed final retreat. In all three dev trials the red cube still ended 5.7–8.3 cm off centre from yellow. I did not read candidate 4's traces or keyframes, so I don't know why. The likely causes are the red cube being knocked or dropped while placing, or the sag correction at the placement spot not holding, but both are guesses.

I saved a library note with the query and release-height fixes. The five held-out trials for candidate 4 are running, and I didn't wait for them. I expect it to fail them for the same red-cube misplacement.
